why: Locations behave like a set of occupied slots: each move removes movedFrom[i] and inserts movedTo[i]. A hash set gives O(1) per move, and sorting at the end gives the required ascending output.
hints: Do you need to know which piece of data is where, or only which locations are occupied?
Only occupancy matters. Keep a set; a move is remove(from) then add(to), and the guarantees promise from is occupied and to is free.
Set of locations, apply moves in order in O(m), return sorted(set) in O(n log n).
pitfalls: Moves must be applied in order: data can move into a location and later out of it again (1 to 4 then 4 to 7).
A location can be emptied and filled again later (5 to 1 after 1 moved away).
Return the result sorted ascending, not in insertion order.
statement:
X keeps its data on servers at n distinct locations, given in locations. During the year the data is moved m times: in operation i (in order) the data at movedFrom[i] moves to movedTo[i]. It is guaranteed that at that moment there is data at movedFrom[i] and no data at movedTo[i].

Return the locations that hold data after all moves, in ascending order.

Worked example: locations = [1, 5, 2, 6], movedFrom = [1, 4, 5, 7], movedTo = [4, 7, 1, 3]

  • Start: {1, 2, 5, 6}
  • 1 to 4: {2, 4, 5, 6}
  • 4 to 7: {2, 5, 6, 7}
  • 5 to 1: {1, 2, 6, 7}
  • 7 to 3: {1, 2, 3, 6}

Answer: [1, 2, 3, 6].
constraints:
• 1 <= n, m <= 10^5 (not stated in the source; reasonable bounds)
  • 1 <= locations[i], movedFrom[i], movedTo[i] <= 10^9 (not stated in the source)
  • locations has distinct values; movedFrom and movedTo have length m.
